title: Significant Figures and Scientific Notation

findings.finding: These questions require interpreting and calculating with scientific notation before that representation has been introduced.
findings.breakdown: Students must use 1.67 × 10^-24 and 7.22 × 10^19 in calculations. The preceding teaching supplies isolated powers of ten and ordinary decimal conversions, but does not explain coefficients multiplied by powers of ten.
findings.checked: Searched all supplied teaching preceding metric-conversions. Scientific notation is first defined on p16, with conversion methods on p18 and p20. The difficulty labels do not supply this missing content.
findings.assumptions: Scientific notation is new within this booklet. A calculator is assumed available; it does not itself explain the representation.

repair.proposal: Move both questions to follow instruction in interpreting scientific notation and using it in calculations. Do not place them immediately after the p16 identification exercises, which do not teach calculation.

findings.doneWhen: Both questions occur after students have been taught to interpret the notation and carry out the required calculations.

findings.finding: The complete conversion of 9 kL to mL is repeated without an explicit instructional purpose.
findings.breakdown: The starting quantity, source unit and destination unit are unchanged.
findings.checked: Compared both complete parts and their shared instructions. Neither states a retrieval or comparison purpose.

repair.proposal: Change p8-q11-c to: Convert 6.4 kL to mL. Answer: 6 400 000 mL.

findings.doneWhen: The later conversion has different values while retaining its structure.

findings.finding: The significant-figure examples depend on place-value rounding without rehearsing it in an opening review.
findings.breakdown: After locating the significant digit, students must recall how the following digit determines rounding and how discarded places are represented. The topic teaches identification of the required place, but delegates the actual rounding to prior knowledge.
findings.checked: Earlier metric teaching and practice do not rehearse rounding. p9 teaches significant-digit identification, and p10 explicitly uses rounding to a named place as its final method step.
findings.assumptions: Whole-number and decimal rounding are prior learning, consistent with the separate Rounding Decimals booklet. No calculator is assumed.

repair.proposal: Before p10-round-information, add: (a) Round 4728 to the nearest hundred. (b) Round 56812 to the nearest ten thousand. (c) Round 0.007846 to four decimal places. (d) Round 739.62 to the nearest whole number. Answers: 4700; 60000; 0.0078; 740. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The review rehearses rounding whole numbers and small decimals, including rounding up and down.

findings.finding: Extend the existing comparison of coinciding rounded values by comparing their numerical errors.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects significant-figure rounding with the distance between an approximation and the original value.
findings.checked: Parts a–c all give 300 000 000, whose difference from 299 792 458 is 207 542. Four significant figures gives 299 800 000, with difference 7542. Only rounding and subtraction are needed.
findings.assumptions: Students can subtract whole numbers; a calculator may be used.

repair.proposal: After part d add: (e) How far is each answer in parts a–c from 299 792 458 m/s? Answer: 207 542 m/s each. (f) Round the original speed to four significant figures. Answer: 299 800 000 m/s. (g) How far is your answer to part f from the original speed? Answer: 7542 m/s.

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up retains the original measurement and separates each question into its own part.

findings.finding: Hold the coefficient fixed while the exponent decreases through zero.
findings.breakdown: The run connects each exponent decrease with division by ten, including the transition through exponent zero.
findings.checked: All conversions are correct. p15 reviews exponent zero and negative powers, and p20 supplies the conversion method. The supplied exercise has no equivalent consecutive run.
findings.assumptions: The parts remain under the existing decimal-form instruction.

repair.proposal: Append one instruction: 'Predict how each answer changes before converting.' Add (j) 4.7 × 10^2; (k) 4.7 × 10^1; (l) 4.7 × 10^0; (m) 4.7 × 10^-1; (n) 4.7 × 10^-2. Answers: 470; 47; 4.7; 0.47; 0.047. Follow with (o) 8.26 × 10^-4, answer 0.000826. Only the exponent varies in j–n.

findings.doneWhen: The run and its unpatterned follow-up appear after p21-q4-i.

findings.finding: The stated integer restriction does not determine unique values of p and q.
findings.breakdown: Dividing the equation by 100 gives 100000p + q = 500004. Both (5, 4) and (4, 100004) satisfy the question, so students cannot determine the intended unique pair.
findings.checked: Worked the equation independently. Earlier scientific-notation conventions do not restrict these two coefficients: the expression is a sum, not a single number explicitly required to be in scientific notation. Part b supplies its own coefficient restriction.
findings.assumptions: The singular instruction intends a uniquely determined pair.

repair.proposal: Replace 'p and q are integers' with 'p and q are integers from 0 to 9.' The unique answer is p = 5 and q = 4.

findings.doneWhen: The written conditions uniquely determine the intended pair.

findings.finding: Extend the existing mass comparison by calculating multiplicative comparisons.
findings.breakdown: Students connect scientific-notation division with comparisons of total populations and individual masses.
findings.checked: The total-mass ratio is (4.8 × 10^11)/(4 × 10^10) = 12. A 60 kg human has the mass of 60/(2 × 10^-6) = 3 × 10^7 ants. Both use the existing context and operations already required by this question.
findings.assumptions: The stated average masses are retained.

repair.proposal: Append optional parts: (f) How many times as much do all the humans weigh as all the ants? Answer: 12 times. (g) How many ants weighing 2 mg each would have the same mass as one 60 kg human? Give your answer in scientific notation. Answer: 3 × 10^7 ants.

findings.doneWhen: The two optional parts follow p24-q10-e.

findings.finding: The combined examples need a short review of scientific-notation conversion and significant-figure rounding.
findings.breakdown: Students must recall decimal relocation, exponent sign and significant-figure rounding while following their combined application.
findings.checked: Both methods are taught earlier, but this topic has no review. The standard's exception for examples combining earlier methods applies even though scientific notation is used immediately beforehand in mixed practice.
findings.assumptions: Prior teaching establishes the methods but does not guarantee fluent recall. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before p26-information, add: (a) Write 630000 in scientific notation. (b) Write 0.00472 in scientific notation. (c) Round 6.374 to three significant figures. (d) Round 1.968 to three significant figures. Answers: 6.3 × 10^5; 4.72 × 10^-3; 6.37; 1.97. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The review rehearses both conversion directions of decimal movement and rounding up and down before the combined examples.

findings.finding: Keep the significant digits fixed while changing magnitude.
findings.breakdown: Students can compare the unchanged rounded coefficient with the changing exponent.
findings.checked: All proposed answers are correct to three significant figures. The method is fully available by p26, and the existing parts do not provide this fixed-digit comparison.
findings.assumptions: The parts remain under the existing scientific-notation and three-significant-figure instruction.

repair.proposal: Append one instruction: 'Predict what will stay the same before calculating.' Add (g) 24230; (h) 2423; (i) 0.2423; (j) 0.002423. Answers: 2.42 × 10^4; 2.42 × 10^3; 2.42 × 10^-1; 2.42 × 10^-3. Follow with (k) 0.0007864, answer 7.86 × 10^-4. Only magnitude varies in g–j.

findings.doneWhen: The run and its unpatterned follow-up appear after p27-q2-f.

findings.finding: These questions introduce calculations with scientific-notation quantities before students have learnt to interpret that representation.
findings.breakdown: Students must interpret coefficients multiplied by powers of ten and combine those quantities through multiplication or division. The preceding metric-prefix table supplies individual powers of ten but does not model this combined use.
findings.checked: All preceding teaching and practice were checked. Scientific-notation interpretation appears on p16, conversions on p18 and p20, and scaffolded calculations involving masses and populations in p24-q10.
findings.assumptions: Scientific notation is new learning in this booklet. A calculator may support the arithmetic, but does not supply the meaning of the representation.

repair.proposal: Move both questions into mixed practice immediately after p24-q10, where scientific-notation interpretation, conversions and scaffolded calculations have preceded them.

findings.doneWhen: Both questions follow the scientific-notation teaching and p24-q10.

findings.finding: Use an existing number to expose the effect of rounding an intermediate result.
findings.breakdown: Successive rounding can change the digit that controls the final rounding decision.
findings.checked: Using the existing value 821.2749: rounding to six significant figures gives 821.275; rounding that to five gives 821.28; direct rounding to five gives 821.27. Only the topic's rounding method is needed.
findings.assumptions: This is an optional follow-up to part f.

repair.proposal: Append: (j) Round the number in part f, 821.2749, to six significant figures. Answer: 821.275. (k) Round your answer to (j) to five significant figures. Answer: 821.28. (l) Round the original number directly to five significant figures. Answer: 821.27. (m) Explain why (k) and (l) differ. Answer: the first rounding changes the thousandths digit from 4 to 5, so the subsequent rounding goes up.

findings.doneWhen: The optional parts use the existing number and compare successive rounding with direct rounding.
